name: Haunted School Night
blurb: Locked in school overnight, a ghost story, and an explanation that almost works
title: Haunted School Night: Horror Comedy Skit Script for 5
description: A 5-minute horror comedy skit script for 5: students locked in school at night find a spooky mystery with a reasonable explanation, almost. Free to perform.
h1: Haunted School Night: a 5-Minute Horror Comedy Skit Script for 5 People
logline: Four students stay late to finish an art project and wake up locked inside their dark school. A moan in the walls, footsteps at the door and a name appearing on the whiteboard make the old ghost story feel very real. Then someone turns on a light and explains everything. Almost everything.
setting: A dark classroom at night. Props: a phone torch, a whiteboard and marker, a head torch or desk lamp, a cloth, a water bottle, a ring of keys, overalls or a work jacket.

roles.name: Zoe
roles.note: Student, any gender (the name on the board can be changed to match). The calm leader, until that name appears.

roles.name: Ben
roles.note: Student, any gender. The scared one. Fell asleep on the paint table and got everyone locked in.

roles.name: Ivy
roles.note: Student, any gender. Knows every ghost story and tells them at the worst moment. Gets the last scare.

roles.name: Max
roles.note: Student, any gender. Practical, holds the only phone with a torch.

roles.name: Mr. Hale
roles.note: Older adult, written as a man (use Mrs. Hale if needed). Kind, slow-moving caretaker with a perfect explanation.

script.scene: SCENE 1 – A dark classroom, late at night

script.action: Darkness. Torch light from a phone. ZOE, BEN, IVY and MAX creep in. Max pulls at the door handle. It does not open.

script.say: Locked. It's locked. We're locked in.
This is your fault. "Let's finish the art project, it'll take ten minutes."
It did take ten minutes. Then you fell asleep on the paint table.
I was resting my eyes.
Everyone stop. My phone is on four percent. Let's just call someone.
No signal. There's never signal in this room.
So we wait till morning. It's fine. It's a school. Nothing happens in a school at night.

script.sfx: A long, low moan from somewhere in the walls.

script.say: What was that?
Nothing. Pipes. Old buildings make noises.
That pipe sounded sad.
You know the story. The girl who stayed late in this room years ago and never went home.
That is a story the older kids tell the new kids.
She used to whisper the names of the people who would be next.
Fine. That's quite a sad pipe.

script.action: Footsteps outside, slow and heavy, getting closer. They stop right outside the door.

script.say: Nobody breathe.
I can't not breathe!

script.action: The footsteps go away. Silence. They let go of each other.

script.say: Okay. There's a person in the building. A person is good. People have keys.
Or the person is not a person.

script.action: Max shines the phone at the whiteboard. Written on it, large: ZOE.

script.say: That wasn't there before.
It's your name.
I know it's my name, Ben!
The names of the people who would be next.
My phone.
I want my mum.
Everyone hold hands. We're going to the door, together, slowly.

script.sfx: The moan again, very close. Footsteps, right inside the room now.

script.action: A bright light snaps on, a head torch, shining in their faces. All four scream. The light belongs to MR. HALE, an older caretaker in overalls, holding a cloth.

script.say: Ah. Good evening. I thought I heard mice.

script.action: The four stare at him, still holding each other.

script.say: You're... you're a person.
Last time I checked. What are you four doing here at midnight?
We got locked in. And there's a ghost. It moans.
That's the heating. Comes on at eleven. Every night it groans like an old dog. I keep telling the office.
And the footsteps?
Me, doing my rounds. These boots are older than you.
Then explain the board. It wrote Zoe's name.

script.action: Mr. Hale walks to the board, laughs softly, and picks up a water bottle from the desk underneath it.

script.say: That's not a ghost. That's lost property. Somebody left this water bottle in here with Zoe on the label. I write the name up so the owner sees it in the morning.

script.action: The four slowly let go of each other. Embarrassed laughter.

script.say: My water bottle. I've been looking for that all week.
I knew it was a water bottle.
You did not.
What about the girl? The one who never went home?
Oh, that one. She went home. She was just very late for dinner. Her mother told that story for years, and it got bigger every time.
So there's no ghost.
There's a lot of dust, a broken heater and four very tired students. That's all I've got.
I am never staying late again.
Come on, then. I'll let you out the side door. Here, take a torch.

script.action: He hands Max a small torch and walks them to the door. He unlocks it with a key from a large ring. Max, Ben and Zoe hurry out, laughing with relief. Ivy stops at the door.

script.say: Thank you, Mr. Hale. Will you be all right on your own all night?
Oh, I'm never on my own. There's always the night cleaner. Mrs. Pell. She does the top floor.
I thought you were the night cleaner.
Me? No. I'm retired.
Since when?
Nineteen eighty-seven.

script.action: He switches off the head torch. Darkness.

script.sfx: From the walls, a long, low moan.

script.say: Guys? Guys, wait for me!

ul: Turn off the room lights or close the curtains; a single phone torch is the whole lighting design. Give a student a second phone offstage to work the head torch moment.
Write ZOE on the board before the show and cover it with a sheet of paper. On the squeak, a hidden student or Mr. Hale behind the board pulls the paper down.
Sound cues can be made live offstage: a low hum through a cardboard tube for the moan, heavy steps on a hard floor, a marker squeak on a spare board.
When Mr. Hale's light snaps on, all four scream and clump together. Rehearse the clump so nobody gets knocked over.
For the ending, Mr. Hale switches off the light on the last word, the moan plays in darkness, and Ivy's line comes from the dark. Then running steps and silence.
The game is three spooky events, each closer and more personal: a sound in the walls, steps at the door, a name on the board. Pause after each and let the fear grow.
Keep the comedy in the reactions, not the scares. Ben's lines should be honest panic; Zoe's patience runs out a bit more each time.
Mr. Hale is warm and ordinary. Each explanation is calm and complete, so the audience relaxes with the students.
The final exchange is all timing: a real beat before Since when, then Mr. Hale answers gently, as if it is the most normal thing in the world.
Horror here is creepy, not frightening. No jumping at the audience and no screaming at the very end; the scare is the idea, not the noise.
Move it to an office building, a museum after closing or a shopping centre, with a night security guard instead of a caretaker.
With a bigger cast, add Mrs. Pell, who appears at the very end at the door, holding a mop and smiling, before blackout.
Different ending: the students check the school's old staff photo the next morning and find Mr. Hale in it, waving.

prompts.keyframe: Four teenagers huddled together in a dark classroom at night, one phone torch lighting their worried faces, a whiteboard behind them, deep shadows, wide shot, creepy but playful, cinematic still, 16:9

Wide shot, a bright head torch suddenly switches on and shines at four students who scream and clump together, then an old caretaker steps forward smiling
Close-up of a kindly old caretaker in a head torch smiling gently, then switching off the light into total darkness, quiet creepy ending

faq.q: Is Haunted School Night too scary for younger students?
faq.a: No. Nothing violent happens and there is no gore. The spooky moments are sounds and a name on a board, all explained, and the ending is a gentle chill rather than a fright. It suits ages ten and up.

faq.q: How do we make the name appear on the board?
faq.a: Write it before the show and cover it with paper taped at the top. On the squeak, someone behind the board or under a desk pulls the paper away. In a very dark room, Max's torch only finds it after it is uncovered.

faq.q: Can we film it or enter it in a drama festival?
faq.a: Yes. The script is free under CC BY 4.0 for stage, festivals and videos, including monetised channels. Credit "Script: cv.cm".
